title: Determinants of Diagnostic Conversion from Unipolar Depression to Bipolar Disorder: A Retrospective Case-Control Study
content: Background: Distinguishing unipolar depression (UD) from bipolar disorder (BD) re-mains a critical diagnostic challenge. In resource-constrained public healthcare systems characterised by extended outpatient follow-up intervals, diagnostic conversion frequently occurs unmonitored. This study investigated clinical, familial, and pharmacological determinants of diagnostic conversion within a multi-ethnic Southeast Asian setting. Methods: Using a retrospective, unmatched case-control design at a major Malaysian tertiary academic medical centre (2016-2025), we analysed 420 vali-dated patient records (140 cases; 280 unmatched controls). Familial liabilities, clinical course features, and psychotropic exposures were evaluated using univariable and multivariable logistic regression. Results: In the primary multivariable analysis (N = 418), a confirmed family history of BD was the strongest independent determinant of diagnostic conversion (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 4.80, 95% CI [2.38, 10.1], p < 0.001). In a secondary hierarchical model, conversion odds scaled from second-degree or dis-tant relatives (aOR = 3.76, 95% CI [1.43, 10.7], p = 0.009) to first-degree relatives (aOR = 6.00, 95% CI [2.32, 17.0], p < 0.001). Prior antidepressant exposure showed an inverse association with conversion (aOR = 0.23, 95% CI [0.08, 0.64], p = 0.006), likely reflecting confounding by indication. Within the female sub-cohort (n = 320), younger age at index date was independently associated with conversion (aOR = 0.96, 95% CI [0.93, 0.99], p = 0.014). Conclusions: Despite retrospective, single-centre limitations, these findings validate familial BD history and younger female index age as accessible clinical markers within an upper-middle-income Southeast Asian setting. Systematic screening for these factors may support closer outpatient monitoring, while future multi-centre registries and health economic studies are warranted to guide early intervention.
